entities.summary:
Jean Weir (died April 22, 1670) was a Scottish woman executed for witchcraft, whose case is inextricably linked to the sensational trial and execution of her brother, Major Thomas Weir, a prominent Edinburgh citizen. Her fate, intertwined with the dramatic accusations against her sibling, illuminates the intense religious fervor, social anxieties, and legal mechanisms of witchcraft prosecution in 17th-century Scotland, a period marked by some of Europe's most severe witch hunts. Her story provides a grim window into the vulnerability of individuals, particularly women, to accusations fueled by confession under duress and societal paranoia.

Jean Weir's arrest and subsequent confession were triggered by her brother Thomas Weir's dramatic public confession of incest, bestiality, and witchcraft in April 1670. After Thomas's confession, Jean was also taken into custody and, under interrogation, admitted to various acts of witchcraft, including using a magical spinning wheel and engaging in an incestuous relationship with her brother. These confessions, extracted in the highly charged atmosphere of the Scottish legal system, were central to her conviction. Both siblings were tried before the High Court of Justiciary in Edinburgh; Jean was found guilty based on her own testimony and executed by hanging on April 22, 1670, just days before her brother met a similar fate, burned at the stake.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jean Weir's case, while not individually world-changing, is significant as part of the notorious Weir trials, which became a prominent example of judicial witchcraft persecution in 17th-century Scotland, contributing to the historical understanding of societal fear and legal practices of the era. Her execution highlights the vulnerability of women to accusations and the severe consequences of religious and social anxieties.
